## Why the Sky Is Blue

Sunlight contains all the colors of the visible spectrum, but when it enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with the tiny gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen) that are much smaller than the wavelength of visible light. These collisions cause the light to scatter in all directions through a process called **Rayleigh scattering**. Because this scattering is strongly wavelength-dependent, shorter wavelengths (blue and violet) are scattered far more efficiently than longer wavelengths (red and orange). As a result, when you look up at any point in the sky away from the Sun directly, you see this scattered blue light arriving from every direction. Interestingly, violet is actually scattered even more than blue, but the sky appears blue rather than violet because the Sun emits less violet light and our eyes are less sensitive to it.

## Rayleigh Scattering Wavelength Dependence

The intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the **fourth power of the wavelength**:

$$I \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$$

This steep dependence means that halving the wavelength increases the scattering by a factor of 16, which is precisely why blue light (~450 nm) scatters roughly 5–6 times more strongly than red light (~650 nm). This same effect explains why sunsets appear red: when sunlight travels through a longer path of atmosphere near the horizon, most of the blue light has already been scattered away, leaving the longer red wavelengths to reach your eyes directly.
